questions.q: What does @zudojs/testing add to Vitest?
questions.explain: It does not run tests; Vitest still does that. It gives you a test double for each moving part of a ZudoJS app, and structural assertions.
options: It replaces Vitest and runs the tests itself
Controllable stand-ins (test doubles) for the clock, logger, event bus, queue, container and HTTP, plus assertions that compare by content
A browser to run tests in

questions.q: Why install vitest and @zudojs/testing with -D?
questions.explain: -D saves them under devDependencies. A production install can leave them out, which keeps the deployed app smaller.
options: Your tests need them, but your running app does not, so they are development dependencies
Because they are not on npm

questions.q: Why does the task service receive now, logger, events and mailer instead of creating them itself?
questions.explain: This is dependency injection. In production you pass () => new Date() and a real mailer; in a test, a test clock and a mock. The service code does not change.
options: So a test can pass doubles it controls, such as a fixed clock and a mailer that sends nothing
Because new Date() does not work in services
So the service can be used without TypeScript

questions.q: Why is a test that reads the real clock a problem for "remind me about overdue tasks"?
questions.explain: A test must give the same result every time. A test clock only moves when you tell it to, so "two days later" takes no time at all.
options: The real clock is too slow
It gives different results on different days, and waiting two real days to test "overdue" is useless
The real clock is always in UTC

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: advance(ms) moves forward by milliseconds: 90 000 ms is 1 minute 30 seconds. add takes days, hours, minutes or seconds, so 2 days and 3 hours later is 12:01:30 on 3 October.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: set(date) jumps to any time, here back to the start. Then 30 minutes and 15 seconds are added.

questions.q: Your test clock started at 1 October 2026. After some add calls you want to go back to the start. What should you call?
questions.explain: Watch out: clock.reset() jumps to the real current time, not back to your start. set(start) goes exactly where you want.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A mock function records every call. calls is a list of argument lists, so calls[1][0] is the first argument of the second call. mockReturnValue sets what it returns.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without mockReturnValue or mockResolvedValue, a mock returns undefined. It still records the call.

questions.q: The mailer's send is async. How do you make its mock return a promise of undefined?
questions.explain: mockResolvedValue(v) makes the mock return a promise that resolves to v, like a real async function. mockRejectedValue(error) makes it fail.

questions.q: The mail server is down. What does this print?
questions.explain: mockRejectedValue makes every call fail with that error, so you can test what your code does when the mail server is down. The failed call is still recorded.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A spy logger is a complete logger that prints nothing and remembers every line in calls, with its method, message and metadata. A test can check what was logged without reading the terminal.

questions.q: You want to record the calls of a real object's method and later put the original back. Which helper fits?
questions.explain: createSpyMethod wraps the real method and records its calls until you call restore(). createStub makes a new object whose methods do nothing unless you write them.
options: createMockFn() assigned over the method, with no way back

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A spy calls the real method, so it still returns hi ada, and it records the call. After restore() the original method is back and works as before.

questions.q: Why does the lesson test through the app's real registerTasks wiring with createTestContainer, instead of building the service by hand?
questions.explain: The test swaps only the outside world (clock, logger, events, mailer, config) and uses the real wiring. So the wiring itself is tested too.
options: It is faster than building by hand
If someone breaks the wiring, for example reading the wrong config key, the test notices; a hand-built service would not
Services cannot be built by hand

questions.q: What does createTestContainer({ overrides: [...] }) give you?
questions.explain: Each override is a token plus the value to use, such as { token: CLOCK, useValue: () => clock.now }. Then you call the app's real registration code on it.
options: A container with no services at all
A started container with your fakes already registered for the listed tokens
A copy of the production container with real services
A container that only works in the browser

questions.q: A test needs tasks.maxOpenTasks to be 1. What does the lesson use?
questions.explain: A test config manager is a real ConfigManager, so the wiring reads it exactly as in production. Changing environment variables or files would leak into other tests.
options: createTestConfigManager({ "tasks.maxOpenTasks": 1 }), a real ConfigManager filled with test values

questions.q: A test starts an HTTP server and forgets to stop it. What can happen?
questions.explain: Open servers, queues and timers keep running after a test. A cleanup manager holds an "undo" function for each, and dispose() runs them all.
options: The next test fails for no clear reason, or Vitest never exits
The server is stopped when the variable goes out of scope
The test is marked as skipped

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: dispose() runs the cleanups in reverse order: last started, first stopped. A server must stop before the queue and database it uses are closed.

questions.q: One cleanup fails. What does this print?
questions.explain: A failing cleanup does not stop the others: the database was still closed. At the end, dispose() reports every cleanup that failed, by name.
options:
reported: 1 of 2 cleanup functions failed: queue
[ 'database' ]

reported: 1 of 2 cleanup functions failed: queue
[]

questions.q: No options are passed to createTestApplication. What does this print?
questions.explain: By default the test application is quiet and repeatable: its logger is a spy logger that prints nothing and records every line in calls, and its clock starts at 1 January 2026, 00:00 UTC, on every run. The container and logger cleanups are already registered, so the count is 2. Pass clock to start on another date.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: This is the trap: JSON.stringify turns every Set into {}, so two different sets look equal. deepEqual compares their members and sees the difference.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object keys may come in any order. Array items must be in the same order. Dates are compared by the time they hold, and 0 ms and 1 ms are different.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: findDifference names the path of the first difference, so you see exactly where it broke: the second tag (index 1) of the task.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An assertion throws when a value is wrong, and names the path of the difference: body.done. The id and title matched; only done did not.
options: Response body mismatch at body.done: expected true, received false.
Response body mismatch: expected true, received false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: assertRejects(fn, text) checks that the async function fails with a message containing text, and returns the error so you can check more, such as its code.

questions.q: The function does not fail. What does this print?
questions.explain: A test that expects a failure must fail itself when no error comes. Otherwise a bug that removes the limit would still pass the test.
options: Expected function to reject, but it did not.
Expected error message to contain "open tasks", got "created".

questions.q: Which assertion checks that a synchronous function throws?
questions.explain: assertRejects is for async functions (a rejected promise). For code that throws right away, use assertThrows.

questions.q: What does an integration test check that a unit test with fakes does not?
questions.explain: The 409 in the lesson comes from a ConflictError thrown deep in the service and mapped to a status by the route. Only a test that runs the whole chain checks that mapping.
options: That one function returns the right value
That the real pieces work together: router, JSON parsing, error mapping and service

questions.q: createHttpTestClient(router) starts a real server the first time you send a request. Why does it use a free port that the operating system picks, not a fixed one like 3000?
questions.explain: Asking the system for any free port (port 0) always works, even when several test files run at once. Register the client with a cleanup manager, { cleanup }, so dispose() stops the server it started.
options: A fixed port may already be used by your dev server or another test; a free port never clashes
A free port disables the network

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: assertCreated checks for 201, and assertResponseBodyContains only checks the fields you list, so both pass. assertResponseStatus(created, 200) fails, because a create answers 201.
options: Response body mismatch at body.done: expected undefined, received false.

questions.q: Why does the Vitest suite create fresh doubles in beforeEach?
questions.explain: Shared state between tests makes the result depend on the order they run in. New doubles for every test keep them independent.
options: So no test can see another test's tasks or clock; each test starts from the same clean state
To make the suite run in parallel

questions.q: Why is cleanup.dispose() in afterEach, not at the end of each test?
questions.explain: A failing assertion throws and skips the rest of the test. Cleanup at the end of the test body would never run, and the open server would break the next test.
options: afterEach runs even when a test fails in the middle, so every server and bus is still closed

questions.q: After the suite passes, the lesson changes clock.add({ days: 2 }) to clock.add({ hours: 12 }). Why?
questions.explain: A test that can never fail proves nothing. After 12 hours nothing is overdue, the reminder count is 0, and the test fails. The clock really drives the result.
options: To check that the test can fail: if it still passed, it would not be testing the time at all
Because 2 days is too long for a test
To fix a bug in the service

questions.q: Why does the lesson also check that no sms.send message was dispatched?
questions.explain: Tests usually check that something happened. Checking that something harmful did not happen catches a different, often more dangerous, class of bugs.
options: A bug that sends an SMS to every user is worse than one that sends nothing, so "not sent" checks matter too
It is required by the message bus

questions.q: Write a tiny test clock. Finish createClock(start): return an object with now() (a new Date of the current time) and add({ days = 0, hours = 0 }) that moves the time forward. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Keep the time as milliseconds in a closure, and only change it in add. Returning a new Date from now() stops callers from changing the clock by accident.

questions.q: Write a recording mock. Finish createMock(returnValue): return a function that records its arguments in fn.calls (an array of argument arrays) and returns returnValue. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Rest parameters (...args) collect all arguments into an array, which the mock stores. Functions are objects, so a calls property can live on the function itself.

questions.q: Make this service testable. Finish createTasks(now): add(title, dueInDays) stores a task due dueInDays after now(), and overdue() returns the titles of tasks whose due date is before now(). Never call new Date() without an argument. The program should print [ 'Buy milk' ].
questions.explain: The service asks now() each time, so the test controls time by changing current. Two days later only the task due after one day is overdue.

questions.q: Write a small cleanup manager. register(fn) stores a cleanup; dispose() runs them all in reverse order, keeps going when one throws, and returns the number that failed. The program should print [ 'server', 'database' ] and then 1.
questions.explain: Last started, first stopped: loop over a reversed copy. A try/catch around each cleanup means one failure does not leave the rest running.

questions.q: JSON.stringify says two different sets are equal. Finish sameSet(a, b) so it compares the members: same size, and every member of a is in b. The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: Sets have no order, so compare membership, not position. Checking the size first catches the case where b has extra members.

questions.q: Finish firstDifference(a, b) for two arrays of strings: return a text like [1]: expected "later", received "urgent" for the first index where they differ (a is received, b is expected), or null if they are equal. The program should print the two lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Loop to the longer length so a missing item also counts as a difference. Naming the index is what makes a failing test quick to fix, like findDifference does.

questions.q: Write your own assertRejects(fn, text): await fn(). If it does not throw, throw an Error with the message did not reject. If it throws but the message does not contain text, throw wrong error. Otherwise return the error. The program should print the three lines in the comments.
questions.explain: Catch the error first, then decide outside the try. If you threw "did not reject" inside the try, your own catch would swallow it and the check would silently pass.

You already have 3 open tasks.
did not reject
wrong error

questions.q: The code under test publishes in three different ways. What does this print?
questions.explain: The test event bus is a real event bus that records inside itself. Whether your code calls publish, publishEvent or emit, and whether it got the double or its bus property, every event lands in published.
